content_html:
A company's market capitalization is the price the stock market puts on the whole business: the share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. This calculator projects how that value could change if it grows at a steady rate, translates the result into the revenue and profit the business would need to support it, and shows what an investment that tracks the company's value might be worth.

How to use this calculator

  1. Current market cap: today's value of all shares. Enter the full dollar figure, so $1 billion is 1000000000.
  2. Annual growth rate and years: the yearly rate you want to test and how far ahead to look. Negative rates are allowed for a shrinking company.
  3. Price-to-sales ratio: market cap divided by yearly revenue. The calculator holds it constant to work out the revenue implied by each future market cap.
  4. Net profit margin: the share of revenue left as profit after all costs and taxes. It turns implied revenue into implied earnings.
  5. Comparison P/E ratio: a price-to-earnings ratio you consider normal for similar companies, used to see what the projected earnings would be worth at that multiple.
  6. Your investment: a starting amount, an optional monthly addition, and, under more options, a dividend yield that is either reinvested or taken as cash.

How the projection works

The market cap compounds once a year: future cap = current cap × (1 + growth rate)years. Revenue is that figure divided by the price-to-sales ratio, and earnings are revenue multiplied by the net margin. Because both ratios are held constant, the implied P/E is simply the price-to-sales ratio divided by the margin. Comparing that number with your comparison P/E is a quick check on whether the starting valuation already looks rich or cheap.

Your investment is assumed to rise and fall with the market cap, which is only true if the share count stays the same. The yearly rate is converted to its monthly equivalent, additions arrive at the end of each month, and dividends are paid quarterly as a quarter of the yearly yield.

Worked example

With the default inputs, a $1 billion company growing 12% a year for 10 years reaches about $3.11 billion, a 3.11× increase. At a price-to-sales ratio of 4, that value implies yearly revenue of about $776.46 million, and a 15% net margin turns it into about $116.47 million of earnings. The implied P/E is 4 ÷ 0.15 ≈ 26.7. At a P/E of 20 the same earnings would support a market cap of only about $2.33 billion, a sign that the projection assumes the market keeps paying a premium.

An investor who puts in $10,000 and adds $200 a month invests $34,000 in total. If the holding grows with the company, it ends at $75,444.49, a gain of $41,444.49 or a 121.90% return on the money put in.

Tips for realistic assumptions

  • Sustained high growth is rare. Tripling a company's value in a decade requires revenue, profit margins and the valuation multiple to combine into a threefold increase, which few businesses manage.
  • Run a cautious, middle and optimistic rate rather than relying on one number, and check which assumption the result is most sensitive to.
  • Share issuance dilutes existing owners and buybacks do the reverse, so a holding can grow more slowly or faster than the company itself.
  • The projection is a straight line. Real stock prices move unevenly, and taxes and fees are not included.

faq.question: What is market capitalization?
faq.answer: Market capitalization is the total value the stock market places on a company's shares. It equals the current share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding, so it changes every time the share price moves.

faq.question: Is market cap the same as what a company is worth?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Market cap only counts the equity. Enterprise value adds debt and subtracts cash, so two companies with the same market cap can have very different total values once their balance sheets are considered.

faq.question: Why does the calculator ask for a price-to-sales ratio?
faq.answer: Holding the price-to-sales ratio steady lets the calculator turn a future market cap into the yearly revenue the business would need to justify it. That makes it easier to judge whether the growth rate you entered is believable.

faq.question: Does my investment grow exactly like the market cap?
faq.answer: Only if the number of shares stays the same. If the company issues new shares your slice of the business shrinks, and if it buys shares back your slice grows, so real returns can differ from the company's overall growth.

faq.question: What growth rate should I enter?
faq.answer: There is no correct figure. Many people look at the company's past revenue growth and analyst expectations, then test a lower and a higher rate to see a range of outcomes rather than a single forecast.

faq.question: Is any of my information saved?
faq.answer: No. Every calculation runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to a server or stored.
